In 1913, bodies of two children were discovered in the Hopetown quarry near Edinburgh. Although the bodies had been in the water at least eighteen months, a man named Sir Sydney Alfred Smith was able to provide the police with vital information. He determined how much time before their deaths the two boys had eaten their last meal, proved that they must have walked to the quarry, and hypothesised that they had been killed by someone they knew.

Some sad(ish) news - I'm taking a break for the Men Losing Weight podcast. 😔⠀
.⠀
The last few weeks have been a little wild. Between our youngest being super ill, what seem like endless trips to the hospital and doctors, juggling caring for the other two boys and trying to be a good hubby for my amazing wife, it's become clear that I need to do less in order to do more of what really counts. ⠀
.⠀
This week I aim to publish the remaining podcasts, upload the last few transformation pics and then log off for a while. I have no idea when (or if) I'll pick this up again, but I definitely hope to in the near future. 🙌⠀
.⠀
Look out for some new episodes in a few days! 😎 And thanks for being part of the MLW journey so far. Keep grindin'! 💪

The Coronation Scot, a British-made steam locomotive, toured the United States and made a stop in Springfield, April 1, 1939.  Inaugurated in 1937, it served the express passenger trains of the London, Midland and Scottish Railway between Glasgow and London. At the Alton station, it drew a crowd of 10,000 people who toured the train. It pulled eight cars on a tour of the central U.S., visiting 38 cities in 14 states before returning to the East Coast. It was featured at the New York World's Fair. Published as Picturing the Past April 15, 2018EnglandÕs Òcrack streamliner,Ó the luxurious Coronation Scot, drew 10,000 people during a visit to Springfield and open house in April 1939. Used on the London to Glasgow route by the London Midland and Scottish rail company, the train was shipped to the United States for exhibition that year at the WorldÕs Fair in New York. It arrived early and set out on a promotional trip through 14 states covering more than 3,100 miles. The modern steam locomotive pulled eight cars and included a sleeping car, which as The Illinois State Journal noted, differed from American sleeping cars in that Òthe passenger sleeps at right angles to the line of travel.Ó The Scot also featured telephones that connected compartments in the cars, cork and asbestos flooring, filtered ventilation, a kitchen car, narrower and shorter cars, and silk and linen appointments in the state rooms. The train could accommodate 173 passengers and it traveled at more than 61 miles per hour. [File/The State Journal-Register]
